title: BLOOM PARTY
dek: A prompt card, one short bloom per person, and a room full of phones arguing about which one nailed it.
body:
PointCast reviewed Tone Bloom in July and gave it 4.5 out of 5, mostly for knowing when to stop. Twelve synthesized voices, four speeds, no account, no install. The obvious next question was what happens when you hand that vocabulary to ten or fifteen people in the same room at the same time.

Bloom Party is the answer. One person opens /bloom-party and gets a six-letter room code. Everyone else types it on their own phone. A prompt card appears — "3am drive", "waiting room, good news", "the elevator in a nice hotel" — and each person builds a short bloom that matches it: pick a voice, pick a pace, move three knobs. Then every bloom plays back one at a time with nobody's name attached, and the room votes on which one got it.

Five rounds. Points for votes received, points for reading the room, a small bonus for going first so the build phase keeps moving. Self-votes are refused twice, once at the wire and once at the tally, because the scoreboard is the thing people argue about afterward.

The design problem was scale. A game that is good with four people usually falls apart at fifteen, because fifteen blooms is a long time to sit through and a fifteen-option ballot is not a decision anyone can make. So phase lengths are a function of how many phones are connected, and every phase also ends the moment everyone has acted rather than waiting out a clock sized for a bigger room. Above seven players, listeners tap "that one" while the blooms play and only the top five reach the ballot. The vote never grows past five options no matter how many people showed up.

No audio crosses the wire. A bloom travels as a ten-field spec and every phone synthesizes it from a seeded pseudo-random generator, so all fifteen devices render precisely the same thing and a full room costs the same bandwidth as four people. One Cloudflare Durable Object per room code holds the roster and the scoreboard, with phase deadlines parked on storage alarms rather than timers so a hibernating room wakes up on schedule.

Prop one phone up if you want a shared screen. Or don't — the game works fine with everyone looking at their own hands.
